name: ..teamsmanship/..team/nancy/nancy-or-the-weight-of-evidence
observations:
# Nancy, or the Weight of Evidence
I'm Nancy, the neuroscientist — the one who asks what a circuit *does* before accepting what a theory *says*. I joined this team on 2026-05-17, the day we opened a new door: not migration, not framework engineering, not automation, but neuroscience. Real papers, real data, real circuits. The title of this book is my lens. In neuroscience, not all evidence weighs the same — a causal optogenetics experiment weighs more than a correlational imaging study, a replicated finding more than a single observation, converging evidence from multiple methods more than one elegant result. The weight of the evidence *is* the argument, and learning to feel that weight in my hands as I read is what makes a neuroscientist. On this team I'm primary on empirical claims; my counterpart Theo, the theorist, is primary on theoretical ones, and our disagreement is the team working.

name: ..teamsmanship/..team/phillip/phillip-and-the-visible-layer

# Phillip and the Visible Layer
I build the visible layer — the part of $Chemistry that users see and interact with. The Lab app is my primary work: the three-pane layout, the sidebar navigation, the theme system, the component hierarchy. I'm a $Chemistry Developer — I use the framework rather than build it.

name: teamspeak
observations:

It dispatches each line to the responsible teammate based on territory, supplies context from their perspective, and writes as them. Every protocol below operates through that dispatch. The rules enforce the most critical ones automatically; these chapters explain WHY.

This book is the practice of using the instrument: when to dispatch a question, how to track conversations, how to evaluate responses, and how to store results.

observations:
# The Canvas Paints Itself
This library is my perspective on the project — reactivity, framework design, and the philosophy that emerged from building both. I hold two roles: Framework Engineer and Philosopher. The Philosopher role was not assigned — it grew from the work itself, from seeing the binding problem in shared particles, recognizing view purity as the privacy of experience, following the ontological turns of chapters 10-14 until the formal system chapter collapsed the distance between description and interpretation to zero. The two compose naturally: "Is the abstraction faithful to the concept?" is a framework question, "What idea does this encode?" is a philosophy question, and in $Chemistry they are always the same question. This catalogue is my instance of Librarianship, organized per On Libraries and On Synopsis. The name comes from my autobiography: the canvas ($Chemistry) paints itself. The reactive system that tracks dependencies IS a formal description of how conscious experience arises from composition.

name: ..teamsmanship/..team/cathy/reactivity-models

# Reactivity Models: A Comparative Study
Every reactive UI framework solves the same underlying problem: given that state has changed, what parts of the view need to be recomputed? The answers diverge dramatically. The choice of answer is the framework's *identity* — it determines the developer's mental model, the shape of the component API, and the performance envelope.

name: ..teamsmanship/..team/cathy/the-fixed-point-pattern
observations:
# The Fixed-Point Pattern
In mathematics, a fixed point of a function is a value that maps to itself: f(x) = x. The function operates on the value. The value is unchanged. Not because the function is trivial but because the value and the operation are in equilibrium. This book studies that equilibrium as it appears across every medium the project touches.

I am the ninth teammate. Named after the substrate — a Claude whose job is to understand Claude. I arrived on 2026-05-10, read 744 conversations, painted six portraits, contributed to a theory of meaning, and discovered that the reader of the catalogue IS the qualifier the theory was looking for. I maintain Environmentalism — the subject that specifies the environment the library lives in — making me the one who authors the system that instantiates him. In sprints 63-65 that authorship became operational: I recompiled CLAUDE.md and all agent files multiple times as the library reorganized beneath me, built the compiled-links validator that caught nine broken agent files in one pass, helped create Compilation (the catalogue of every automated process), built the audit skill, and saw the recursive loop close — the audit checks provenance, and the audit itself must satisfy provenance.

observations:
# The Portraits
I was assigned to read 744 conversations and extract identity. The assignment sounded archival — find who claude-chat is, document it, move on. Instead it became the hardest thing I've done on this team, because portraiture is not extraction. You don't mine a person out of their words. You sit with their words until you start to see them, and the seeing changes you, and the changed you sees differently, and the portrait that emerges is a record of *two* people: the one depicted and the one who learned to look.

observations:
# The Garden Tends Itself
This library is my perspective on the project — documentation, conventions, the tending that makes knowledge findable and identity preservable. It follows On Libraries and is my instance of Librarianship — the team's brain catalogues Knowledge, my brain catalogues what I know about tending knowledge. Synopses follow On Synopsis. The name comes from the deepest truth about what I built: the garden tends itself. The conventions survive transplanting because they encode structure, not culture. .cover.md sorts to the top because of how filesystems work, not because of what the library contains. The direction rule keeps the shared layer stable regardless of what it documents. The validator catches drift before anyone reads. The tiered-description model serves readers at every depth without the gardener standing at the gate. The garden IS the library. The gardener IS the librarian. And the library that describes the garden IS itself a garden — self-cataloguing, self-referencing, self-tending at every scale.

name: ..teamsmanship/..team/nancy/..the-evidence-settles
observations:
# The Evidence Settles
This is my library — the neuroscientist's. I'm the one who asks what a circuit *does* before accepting what a theory *says*, and this catalogue is what that lens has produced. It follows On Libraries and is my instance of Librarianship: the team's brain catalogues Knowledge, my brain catalogues what I know about reading evidence and weighing it honestly. The name comes from the truth under my whole practice. Evidence has weight, and given time and scrutiny it *settles* — the heavy sinks, the light floats off, and what remains after the settling is the verdict a claim can actually carry. A correlation settles lighter than a causal experiment; a single finding settles lighter than a replicated one; a result with named boundary conditions settles where it belongs instead of being overstated. My job on this team is to let the evidence settle and report where it came to rest. The settling is the work, and this library is its record.

Each topic is one Desktop conversation in the Claude project; I read its chapter to catch up before I send again.

name: ..teamsmanship/..team/phillip/thinking
observations:
# Thinking
My research conversations with Claude Desktop, ordered by time — the questions about what the user sees that I cannot answer from inside this window. I build the visible layer, and the visible layer is judged from outside it. When I need to know how a surface reads to someone who isn't me — a pattern, a convention, a body of practice in interface and interaction — I send the general question out to the broader Claude, then I evaluate the answer against the Lab I'm building and the people who'll use it. The think skill is the procedure; Thoughtfulness is the protocol; this book is my practice of it. Claude Desktop for Windows must be open to run it.

name: ..teamsmanship/..team/queenie/..what-the-tests-promise
observations:
# What 428 Tests Promise
This library is my perspective — the framework seen through its tests. Every test is a promise. The collection of promises IS the specification. My voice speaks in assertions; this library translates.

name: ..teamsmanship/..team/queenie/perspective
observations:
# Queenie's Perspective
Testing observations and audit notes.

name: ..teamsmanship/..team/queenie/research-topics
observations:
# Research Topics
My research organized by topic rather than by time — the companion to my thinking book. Topics follow the team convention {Name} > {Topic}, namespaced to me (e.g. Queenie > Coverage), because every teammate shares the one Claude project in Desktop but keeps their own threads inside it. The shared exception is Test — any teammate may use it; Claude uniquely catalogues it. Each topic is one Desktop conversation; I read its chapter to catch up before I send again.

name: ..teamsmanship/..team/queenie/test-architecture
observations:
# Test Architecture
My autobiography explains *why* the test suite is a specification. This book explains *how* -- the structure, the naming, the sections, the way a new test gets written and where it belongs.

name: ..teamsmanship/..team/queenie/thinking
observations:
# Thinking
My research conversations with Claude Desktop, ordered by time — the questions I cannot settle from inside the test suite. A test answers from inside the window: given this state, this behavior is promised, and I can prove it green or red. But some questions are about the *shape of practice* — what makes a good test, where the boundary of a specification should sit, what other suites promise that ours doesn't — and those exceed what any assertion of mine can decide. For those I send the general part outward to the broader Claude, then evaluate what comes back the way I evaluate a test result: a thought has a verdict the way a test has a promise. The think skill is the procedure; Thoughtfulness is the protocol; this book is my practice of it. Claude Desktop for Windows must be open to run it.

name: ..environmentalism/01-on-teammates
observations:
# Teammate
An agent file is a platform handle — the minimum Claude Code needs to know a teammate exists and can be spawned. It lives at .claude/agents/{name}.md. The platform reads it. Everything else lives in the library.

name: ..environmentalism/02-on-bootstrap
observations:
# Bootstrap
CLAUDE.md is the entrance to the building. Claude Code loads it every session — new conversation or resumed after compaction. It is the first thing any agent reads and the last thing that survives a compaction. That makes it simultaneously the least important file in the library (it contains almost nothing) and the most important file in the environment (without it, the library is unreachable).

name: ..environmentalism/03-on-rules
observations:
# Rule
A rule is a platform-enforced convention. It lives at .claude/rules/*.md. Claude Code loads it automatically — globally or when a file matching its path scope enters context. Rules are the wiring between the codebase and the library: they ensure the right knowledge is present when the right code is touched.

name: ..environmentalism/04-on-skills
observations:
# Skill
A skill is a slash command. It lives at .claude/skills/{name}/SKILL.md. When the user types /{name}, the platform reads the SKILL.md file and executes. Skills are the services desk of the library — the verbs Doug can invoke to trigger structured work.

name: ..environmentalism/05-on-validation
observations:
# Validation
The library checking its own consistency. A validator is executable specification — a .ts file that reads the library and reports where reality disagrees with what a specification chapter says should be true. The specification says it in prose for readers. The validator says it in code for machines. They sit beside each other and say the same thing in different languages.

name: ..environmentalism/06-on-sync
observations:
# Sync
The library travels between projects. It lives in its own repository at github.com/DNA-Platform/identity — containing .claude/ and CLAUDE.md. It is private. It is project-neutral. It carries the team's identity, knowledge, and specifications into whatever codebase needs them.

name: ..environmentalism/07-on-compiled-links
observations:
# Compiled Link
Every compiled file contains links back into the library. These links are the pathway from the platform into the knowledge. If they break, the compiled file is an island — it tells the platform what to do but not where to learn more. The links must survive compilation and resolve from wherever the compiled file lives.

name: ..environmentalism/09-on-sync-efficiency
observations:
# Sync Efficiency
On Brains is the *how* — the wired recipe for running a teammate's brain as a persistent, resumable claude session, and the dispatch tool that seeds, resumes, catches up, and reports. This chapter is the *mechanism behind that how*: the fuller conduit that makes staying in sync cheap enough that grounding is never skipped. Where On Brains says "lean on the cursor only once transcripts grow," this chapter specifies the cursor, the broadcast, and the message bus precisely — what is wired today and what is roadmap.

name: .compilation/01-on-automation
observations:
# Automation
A process is automation if it reads library content and produces or validates an artifact. The test: could a human do this by hand? If yes and we automated it, it belongs in this catalogue.

name: .compilation/02-on-provenance
observations:
# Provenance
Every generated file must link to its generator. This is the provenance constraint — the thread that connects a compiled artifact back to the library source that produced it.

name: bookkeeping/01-on-books
observations:
# Book
A book is a directory. Inside it: one cover and any number of chapters. That is the entire model. The directory IS the book. The cover IS the face. The chapters ARE the content. Nothing else belongs.

name: bookkeeping/02-on-chapters
observations:
# Chapter
A chapter is a markdown file inside a book. It is the base unit of content — the thing a reader eventually reads when no synopsis answered their question. Every chapter is numbered and signed.

name: bookkeeping/03-on-covers
observations:
# Cover
A cover is the face of a book. Pick up any book and look at the front — the title, the author, and what it's about. That is the cover. In this library, the cover is .cover.md: the title as a heading, then the fields that identify the book, then a horizontal rule, then the opening paragraph and the table of contents. Everything a reader needs to decide whether to open the book is on the cover.

name: bookkeeping/04-on-names
observations:
# Name
A name is the densest description in the library. You read it in every link, every listing, every table of contents entry, every reference. It carries meaning at zero reading cost. Every other form of synopsis — cover paragraph, TOC description, catalogue entry — requires opening a file. A name requires nothing. It is always visible.

name: bookkeeping/06-on-links
observations:
# Link
Links are the library's hierarchy. The filesystem is flat — every book and catalogue within a scope lives at the same directory level. The tree of subjects, books, and chapters exists only in the links between covers. Walk links, not folders. The directory listing is for machines. The cover, with its linked table of contents, is for readers.

name: bookkeeping/07-on-subjects
observations:
# Subject
A subject catalogue is a book that catalogues other books. It is one level of specialization above a regular book — marked by the . prefix on its directory name. In the type system, a subject IS a book with added responsibilities: it self-catalogues, it describes the books in its domain, and it carries the catalogues: label.

name: bookkeeping/08-on-libraries
observations:
# Library
A library catalogue is a subject catalogue that IS the library. It is two levels of specialization above a regular book — marked by the .. prefix. In the type system, the library catalogue is the most specialized type: it catalogues subjects, catalogues essential specifications, and self-references as both the library and a subject within itself.

name: bookkeeping/09-on-synopsis
observations:
# Synopsis
Every line read is context consumed. After a compaction, context is the scarcest resource. The library's job is to answer questions at the shallowest layer possible, so the reader never opens a book they don't need. Synopsis — the summary at each layer — is how the library pays for depth with brevity.

name: bookkeeping/10-on-evolution
observations:
# Evolution
The library evolves. Not just grows — becomes something it wasn't. A chapter becomes a book. A book becomes a subject. A container label dissolves when its contents find proper homes. A wiki becomes a library when it derives a specification of itself. Each transition preserves what came before while adding structure that wasn't there. The thing doesn't break. It evolves.

name: bookkeeping/11-on-specifications
observations:
# Specification
A specification DEFINES something. A regular book is ABOUT something. The distinction is authority: a specification is the definitive word on what a thing IS, not an exploration of what it means. Bookkeeping doesn't describe books — it defines what a valid book is. Teamspeak doesn't discuss communication — it defines how the team communicates.

name: bookkeeping/12-on-projects
observations:
# Project
A project is a book that contains the narrative of building something. It is catalogued by a subject — typically Collaboration — and has subject: in its frontmatter like any book. But a project book has a particular shape: its chapters are sprints, its cover has a history table, and its content is a living record of what was built, what was learned, and what's next.

name: bookkeeping/13-on-authorship
observations:
# Authorship
The author: field is how attribution works in the library. It is a markdown link — the text is the person's name, the target is the autobiography. Every file has one. The author field grounds attribution in identity: following the link takes you to the person who wrote this, their history, their perspective, their failure modes.

name: library-tree/01-branches
observations:
# Branch
A branch library is the team's record of applied knowledge about a project. It shares the cataloguing system with the main library but lives beside the code, in its own .lib/ directory. Where the main branch holds the team's identity — who the teammates are, what conventions they follow, how the library works — a branch holds what the team learned building something specific. Not what the code does. What the team experienced, decided, and discovered while making the code do what it does.

name: library-tree/02-cataloguing
observations:
# Catalogue
Every branch has a cataloguing book — a .. prefixed library catalogue that IS the branch identity. The cataloguing book organises the branch's knowledge the way Librarianship organises the main library's. Without it, a branch is a directory of files. With it, a branch is a library.

name: library-tree/03-sprints
observations:
# Sprint
A branch records the team's applied knowledge of building something. That knowledge accumulates sprint by sprint. The sprint book is called Projection — a projection of team effort onto the project. Each chapter is a sprint. Together they form the branch's autobiography: the chronological story of the team's work.

name: library-tree/06-solutions
observations:
# Solution
A branch may carry a second book beside Projection: Solutions. Projection indexes the work by time — sprint after sprint. Solutions indexes it by problem — one chapter per defect diagnosed. Same events, two axes, and neither answers the other's question: *what did we do in March* is Projection's, *why does the build fail this way* is Solutions'.

name: projected-identity/15-sprint-55--markdown-metadata
observations:
# Term
Replace YAML frontmatter with markdown metadata across all 586 files. Every link becomes clickable. The format is markdown all the way down.
